impact_summary: GitLab.com was unavailable or severely degraded for an extended period following the January 31st database incident. Database data created between January 31st 17:20 UTC and 23:30 UTC was permanently lost, including an estimated 5000 projects, 5000 comments, and roughly 700 users (Git repositories and wikis were not affected). Recovery required restoring from a staging snapshot taken about 6 hours before the outage, with copying taking approximately 18 hours, and the service was fully restored around February 1st 18:00 UTC.

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving (continuous archiving to object storage) for the production PostgreSQL primary so replicas can catch up without manual re-synchronisation after falling behind.
Verify and fix the pg_dump backup procedure so the client binary version always matches the production PostgreSQL major version, decoupled from the presence of a local data directory.
Add automated restore tests that regularly restore the latest backup into a scratch environment and verify row counts and integrity, failing loudly if backups are missing or empty.
Configure backup and cronjob failure alerts to use a delivery path that passes DMARC (or a non-email alerting channel) and add alerting on the absence of new backup objects in the S3 bucket.
Enable Azure disk snapshots for all production database servers and document the expected restore time from each storage account location.

Add guardrails to destructive database operations, such as requiring explicit confirmation of hostname/role and a safe-mode wrapper that refuses to remove data directories on a host reporting primary role.
Update engineering runbooks to document that pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to begin streaming, including expected output and how to verify progress from the primary side.
Review and correct production PostgreSQL configuration, including max_connections, against kernel semaphore limits, and add a configuration audit to detect values that would block restarts.
Fix the background account-removal job so it performs soft deletion and rate-limits bulk data removal to avoid large database load spikes.
Introduce read-load distribution (e.g., connection pooling and read replicas via pgpool-II or equivalent) to reduce dependence on a single primary database.
Document a disaster recovery runbook with an explicit restore order, validated restore options, and designated decision-makers so engineers are not searching for backups under pressure.
Use premium or equivalently performant storage for staging or dedicated recovery hosts where restoration speed matters, and measure restore throughput as part of DR testing.
Add host identity indicators (for example, prominent role labels in shell prompts and tooling) to reduce the chance of running destructive commands on the wrong server.
Scale the public monitoring dashboard so it stays available during high-traffic incidents, decoupled from the infrastructure it reports on.
